concepts.name: Client-specified data selection
aliases: asking for exactly what you need
concepts.summary: Explain that a GraphQL client lists the fields it wants and the response mirrors that shape, avoiding fixed server-defined payloads.

concepts.name: Single endpoint model
concepts.summary: Describe how all operations go to one endpoint, with the operation in the request body rather than in the URL path and HTTP method.

concepts.name: Schema as contract
concepts.summary: Understand that the schema defines the types and operations available and acts as the contract between client and server.

concepts.name: Scalar and object types
concepts.summary: Recall the built-in scalars (Int, Float, String, Boolean, ID) and that object types group named fields.

concepts.name: Query field selection
concepts.summary: Read and write a simple query with nested selection sets and understand the JSON response it returns.

concepts.name: Three operation types
concepts.summary: Name query, mutation and subscription and state what each is for: reading, writing and receiving live updates.

misconceptions.text: GraphQL is a database or storage technology.
GraphQL needs a separate URL for each resource like REST.
A GraphQL query returns all fields of an object automatically.

concepts.name: Arguments and variables
concepts.summary: Pass arguments to fields and use typed variables with a separate variables payload instead of string-building queries.

concepts.name: Non-null and list modifiers
concepts.summary: Read type notation such as [String!]! and predict what nullability means for a response.

concepts.name: Aliases and fragments
concepts.summary: Use aliases to rename or repeat fields and fragments to reuse selection sets.

concepts.name: Schema definition language
concepts.summary: Write a small schema in SDL defining object types, Query and Mutation root types, enums and relationships.

concepts.name: Mutations with input types
concepts.summary: Write mutations that take input object types and select the fields of the changed data in the response.

concepts.name: Resolver basics
concepts.summary: Implement a resolver function per field that receives parent, arguments and context and returns data.

concepts.name: GraphQL error responses
concepts.summary: Interpret the response's data and errors keys, including that HTTP 200 can still carry errors.

misconceptions.text: Fields in a schema are nullable only if marked with an exclamation mark.
Any failed GraphQL operation returns a 4xx or 5xx HTTP status.
Variables are just string interpolation done by the client library.

concepts.name: Resolver chain execution
concepts.summary: Trace how the executor resolves fields level by level, passing each parent result to child resolvers, and analyse the cost.

concepts.name: N+1 problem and batching
concepts.summary: Diagnose N+1 queries caused by per-item resolvers and fix them with request-scoped batching and caching.

concepts.name: Interfaces and unions
concepts.summary: Model polymorphic data with interfaces and unions and query them using inline fragments and __typename.

concepts.name: Context and authorization
concepts.summary: Place authentication data in context and enforce authorization in resolvers or business logic layer rather than only at the edge.

concepts.name: Pagination patterns
concepts.summary: Compare offset and cursor-based pagination and design list fields using the connection pattern with edges and pageInfo.

concepts.name: Subscriptions over persistent connections
concepts.summary: Implement a subscription that streams events from a pub/sub source over a persistent transport such as WebSocket.

concepts.name: Client-side caching
concepts.summary: Analyse how clients normalise results by type and id and how this affects cache updates after mutations.

concepts.name: Error and null propagation
concepts.summary: Predict how an error in a non-null field bubbles up to the nearest nullable parent and design schemas accordingly.

misconceptions.text: GraphQL automatically prevents N+1 database queries.
Hiding a field from the UI is sufficient authorization.
Offset pagination is always fine for large, changing lists.

concepts.name: Schema design principles
concepts.summary: Evaluate schema designs against client needs, naming consistency and domain language rather than mirroring database tables.

concepts.name: Mutation payload design
concepts.summary: Judge designs for mutation inputs and payloads, including returning typed domain errors versus top-level errors.

concepts.name: Query cost and depth limiting
concepts.summary: Analyse abuse risks from deeply nested or expensive queries and apply depth, complexity and timeout limits.

concepts.name: Persisted queries and caching
concepts.summary: Analyse how persisted queries and CDN or response caching work given POST-based operations and personalised data.

concepts.name: Schema evolution and deprecation
concepts.summary: Evaluate changes as breaking or non-breaking and manage them with additive change and deprecation instead of versions.

concepts.name: Federation and schema composition
concepts.summary: Analyse how multiple services contribute to one graph through stitching or federation and the tradeoffs in ownership.

concepts.name: Observability and performance tracing
concepts.summary: Use per-field tracing and operation-level metrics to locate slow resolvers and track client usage.

concepts.name: Introspection and security hardening
concepts.summary: Evaluate exposure from introspection, batching and verbose errors and choose appropriate hardening for each environment.

misconceptions.text: A GraphQL schema should map one-to-one to database tables.
GraphQL needs API versions like v1 and v2 for any change.
Disabling introspection is enough to secure a GraphQL API.

concepts.name: Graph architecture governance
concepts.summary: Design an organisation-wide process for schema ownership, review, linting and change validation against real client traffic.

concepts.name: Federation architecture tradeoffs
concepts.summary: Evaluate when a federated gateway, a single server or a backend-for-frontend fits, weighing latency, ownership and failure modes.

concepts.name: Incremental delivery with defer and stream
concepts.summary: Assess incremental delivery of response parts and its effects on client rendering, caching and transport.

concepts.name: Custom directives and schema tooling
concepts.summary: Create directives, schema transforms and code generation pipelines that enforce conventions and type safety end to end.

concepts.name: Query planning and execution optimisation
concepts.summary: Evaluate strategies such as field lookahead, join pushdown and parallel fetching to cut backend load and latency.

concepts.name: Resilience and rate limiting design
concepts.summary: Design cost-based rate limiting, timeouts and fallbacks that degrade gracefully when downstream services fail.

concepts.name: Choosing GraphQL versus alternatives
concepts.summary: Judge when GraphQL, REST or RPC best suits a product given caching, tooling, team structure and client diversity.

misconceptions.text: Federation is always better than a single GraphQL server.
GraphQL is a replacement that makes REST obsolete in every case.
Request-count-based rate limiting is adequate for GraphQL.
